module.title: Propositional Logic
module.description: Module 1 v4 keeps the v3 flow philosophy but adds structured worked-example types: `truth_table_solution` (real table data with reveal-step metadata), `law_step_solution` (rule-based proofs with the exact CPCS222 law names per step), and `passage_analysis` (per-sentence classification for midterm-style passages). Long answers are split into multi-line readable parts. Mermaid diagrams carry display metadata for the frontend. All v3 fields are preserved for backward compatibility.

lessons.title: What Is a Proposition?
lessons.welcome: Logic, mathematical proofs, and even university registration rules all rest on a single atom: a sentence that is definitely true or false. This lesson nails down exactly which sentences qualify.
objectives: Define a proposition and identify its truth value.
Distinguish propositions from questions, commands, exclamations, and open sentences.
Assign propositional variables (p, q, r) to atomic propositions.
Recognize the standard 'not-a-proposition' traps used on labs and exams.

storytelling.speaker: Student
storytelling.text: Professor, why is `x > 5` not a proposition? It looks mathematical.

storytelling.speaker: Professor
storytelling.text: Because x is free. Until you pick a value or quantify x, the sentence has no fixed truth value. Plug in x = 7 → '7 > 5' (true). Plug in x = 2 → '2 > 5' (false). The original is just a TEMPLATE.

flow.title: Proposition
flow.content: A **proposition** is a declarative sentence that is either **true (T)** or **false (F)**, but never both.

Two checks decide whether a sentence is a proposition:

1. It must be **declarative** (a statement, not a question or command).
2. It must have a **definite truth value** right now — no free variables, no missing context.

Both checks must pass. Failing either disqualifies the sentence.

flow.title: Quick gallery
rows: Jeddah is on the Red Sea.

flow.trigger: After the gallery — students often need confirmation on the open-sentence trap.

exchange.speaker: Student
exchange.text: So `x + 2 = 7` is not a proposition because of x?

exchange.speaker: Professor
exchange.text: Right. Free variables disqualify. Plug in x = 5 → '5 + 2 = 7' (true). Plug in x = 1 → '1 + 2 = 7' (false). The original is a template, not a proposition.

flow.title: Don't confuse FALSE with NOT-A-PROPOSITION
flow.content: A wrong claim like 'KAU is in Riyadh' is **still a proposition** — its truth value is just F. The disqualifier is having NO truth value at all, not having the wrong one.

flow.title: Around campus and Absher
items: **Proposition (T):** 'CPCS 222 is offered at King Abdulaziz University.'
**Proposition (F):** 'Tabuk is the capital of Saudi Arabia.'
**Not a proposition:** 'Open Absher and renew your iqama.' (command)
**Not a proposition:** 'Did you pay your STC bill?' (question)
**Not a proposition:** 'x is enrolled in CPCS 222.' (open sentence)

flow.title: Naming atomic propositions
flow.content: Once a sentence passes both checks, we name it with a letter — usually p, q, r, s. Example: let `p` = 'It is raining in Jeddah' and `q` = 'I am at home'. We can now talk about `p ∧ q` ('it is raining in Jeddah AND I am at home') symbolically. Pick a fresh letter for each fresh sentence; never reuse `p` for two different statements.

flow.title: The two-question test
Exam-style passage (midterm Q1 pattern)
flow.source_pattern: Inspired by Spring 2026 midterm Q1 — 'identify the sentences that are not a proposition'.
flow.problem: Read the passage and list the non-propositions.
flow.approach: Walk through each sentence and apply the two-property test (declarative + definite truth value).
flow.passage: Sara reached KAU before her CPCS 222 lecture. The library opens at 7:30 AM. Please silence your phone. 12 is divisible by 4. She wrote x + 5 = 11 in her notebook. Wow, the lecture hall is full today!

sentences.sentence: Sara reached KAU before her CPCS 222 lecture.
sentences.explanation: A factual declarative statement; presumed determined truth value.
Declarative; either matches the actual library hours or not.
Pure arithmetic; truth value is determined.
Free variable x; truth depends on the value of x.

sentences.sentence: Wow, the lecture hall is full today!

flow.thinking_process: Tag each sentence by the two-property test; flag any failure to either property.
step_by_step_solution: Sentence 1: declarative ✓, definite ✓ → Proposition.
Sentence 2: declarative ✓, definite ✓ → Proposition.
Sentence 3: not declarative (command) → NOT a proposition.
Sentence 4: declarative ✓, definite ✓ (T) → Proposition.
Sentence 5: declarative-looking, but has free variable x → NOT a proposition.
Sentence 6: exclamation, not declarative → NOT a proposition.
flow.final_answer: Three non-propositions: the command (#3), the open sentence (#5), and the exclamation (#6).
flow.why_it_works: Each rejected sentence fails one of the two property checks; the rest are clean declaratives with definite truth values.
flow.common_mistake: Marking the open sentence 'x + 5 = 11' as a proposition because it looks mathematical.

flow.title: Lab 01 starter — classification
flow.source_pattern: Inspired by Lab 01 Q1 — proposition classification.
flow.problem:
Decide if each is a proposition; if so, give the truth value.
(a) 'Cairo is the capital of Egypt.'
(b) '5 + 7 = 10.'
(c) 'x + 2 = 11.'
(d) 'Answer this question.'
flow.approach: Apply the two-property test once per item.
flow.thinking_process: Each sentence is independent; classify one at a time.
step_by_step_solution: (a) Declarative ✓ + definite ✓ → Proposition. Truth value: T.
(b) Declarative ✓ + definite ✓ (5 + 7 = 12, not 10) → Proposition. Truth value: F.
(c) Free variable x; no definite truth value → NOT a proposition (open sentence).
(d) Imperative; not declarative → NOT a proposition (command).
flow.final_answer: (a) Proposition, T.  (b) Proposition, F.  (c) Open sentence.  (d) Command.
flow.why_it_works: Every item is filtered through the same two checks; either it passes both or it fails one.
flow.common_mistake: Calling (c) a proposition because it has an equals sign — equations with free variables are still open sentences.

flow.title: Common student mistakes
items: Thinking a **false** sentence cannot be a proposition. False propositions are still propositions.
Treating equations with free variables as propositions. They are open sentences.
Calling a self-referential paradox ('this sentence is false') a proposition — it cannot consistently be T or F.

flow.title: Two-Question Test
flow.content: Declarative? Definite truth value? Both YES → proposition. Anything else: not a proposition.

sections.heading: The two-property test
sections.explanation: A sentence is a proposition iff it is declarative AND has a definite truth value.

sections.heading: Atomic propositions and naming
sections.explanation: Each simple proposition gets a fresh letter (p, q, r, s) for symbolic manipulation.

sections.heading: Exam-style passages
sections.explanation: Mixed sentences must be classified one at a time using the two-property test.

worked_examples.problem: Read the passage and list the non-propositions: 'Sara reached KAU before her CPCS 222 lecture. The library opens at 7:30 AM. Please silence your phone. 12 is divisible by 4. She wrote x + 5 = 11. Wow, the lecture hall is full today!'
step_by_step_solution: Apply the two-property test to each sentence.
'Please silence your phone' — command → not a proposition.
'x + 5 = 11' — open sentence (free x) → not a proposition.
'Wow, the lecture hall is full today!' — exclamation → not a proposition.
The remaining three sentences are propositions.
worked_examples.final_answer: Three non-propositions: command, open sentence, exclamation.
worked_examples.why_it_works: Each rejected sentence fails one of the two property checks.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Marking the open sentence as a proposition because it looks mathematical.

quick_checks.question: Which IS a proposition?
quick_checks.explanation: Declarative with a definite truth value.

quick_checks.question: A false sentence cannot be a proposition.
quick_checks.explanation: A proposition only needs a definite truth value; being false is allowed.

quick_checks.question: Why is 'y > 5' not a proposition?
quick_checks.answer: Because y is free; without a value the sentence has no definite truth value.
quick_checks.explanation: Open sentences become propositions only when their variables are bound or assigned.

key_takeaways: A proposition is a declarative sentence with a definite truth value (T or F).
Questions, commands, exclamations, and open sentences are NOT propositions.
Atomic propositions get fresh letters (p, q, r) for symbolic manipulation.
summary.next: Now we combine atomic propositions using **logical connectives** — the small symbols that act like the verbs of formal logic.

lessons.title: Logical Connectives — The Verbs of Logic
lessons.welcome: Atomic propositions are useful only once we COMBINE them. Four small symbols (¬, ∧, ∨, ⊕) act like the verbs of formal logic.
objectives: Compute the truth value of compound propositions involving ¬, ∧, ∨, ⊕.
Translate English connectives ('and', 'but', 'or', 'either…or but not both') into the right symbol.
Distinguish inclusive ∨ from exclusive ⊕ in everyday English.

storytelling.speaker: Student
storytelling.text: Why do we need separate symbols ∨ and ⊕? English just says 'or'.

storytelling.speaker: Professor
storytelling.text: Because English 'or' is ambiguous. 'You may pay with mada OR Apple Pay' allows both. 'Soup OR salad with the entrée' rules out both. Logic uses ∨ for inclusive and ⊕ for exclusive so every formula has one definite meaning.

flow.content:
Imagine the KAU registration rule:

> _'You may register for CPCS 222 if you passed CPCS 203 **and** your GPA is at least 2.0.'_

This is a compound condition — two atomic conditions joined by **AND**, captured by the symbol **∧**.

flow.title: Negation (¬)
flow.content: **¬p** flips p's truth value. T → F, F → T.

flow.title: Conjunction (∧)
flow.content: **p ∧ q** is true exactly when **both** p and q are true. English 'but' is logically the same as 'and'.

flow.title: Conjunction (p ∧ q)
flow.notes: True only when both are true.

flow.title: Disjunction (∨) — inclusive 'or'
flow.content: **p ∨ q** is true when at least one of p, q is true (including both). This is the inclusive 'or' of mathematics.

flow.title: Disjunction (p ∨ q) — inclusive 'or'
flow.notes: False only when both are false.

flow.title: Exclusive or (⊕)
flow.content: **p ⊕ q** is true when exactly one of p, q is true (but not both).

flow.title: Exclusive or (p ⊕ q)
flow.notes: True when exactly one operand is true.

exchange.speaker: Student
exchange.text: How do I tell when English 'or' is inclusive vs exclusive?

exchange.speaker: Professor
exchange.text: Ask: would the speaker accept BOTH happening? 'You may pay with mada OR Apple Pay' — the cashier doesn't reject you for using both, so it is inclusive ∨. 'Soup OR salad' — picking both is excluded, so it is exclusive ⊕. When in doubt, default to ∨.

flow.title: ∨ vs ⊕ — only one row differs
flow.notes: Both agree on three rows; they disagree only on (T, T).

flow.title: ∨ vs ⊕ around Saudi Arabia
items: **∨:** 'You may pay your STC bill via mada OR Apple Pay.' (both methods OK)
**⊕:** 'Either renew your driver's license on Absher OR at the Muroor office (they share a record).'
**∨:** 'Students who took CPCS 203 OR Math 110 may register.'
**⊕:** 'Either you arrive on time OR you miss the exam — not both.'

flow.title: Operator precedence shortcut
flow.content: When parentheses are missing, **¬** binds tightest. `¬p ∨ q` parses as `(¬p) ∨ q`, NOT `¬(p ∨ q)`.

flow.title: Evaluating a compound proposition
items: 1. Identify the atomic variables and their truth values.
2. Compute innermost subexpressions first (negations, parenthesized parts).
3. Move outward connective by connective.
4. The final value is the truth of the whole expression.

flow.title: Translating English to symbols
flow.source_pattern: Inspired by Lab 01 Q3 — translation with p, q (freezing / snowing).
flow.problem:
Let `p` = 'It is below freezing' and `q` = 'It is snowing'. Translate:
(a) 'It is below freezing **and** snowing.'
(b) 'It is below freezing **but not** snowing.'
(c) 'It is **not** below freezing **and** it is **not** snowing.'
(d) 'Either it is snowing **or** below freezing (or both).'
flow.approach: Map each English connector to a symbol; apply ¬ to whichever piece is being negated.
flow.thinking_process: Each sub-question is an independent translation.
step_by_step_solution: (a) 'and' → ∧. Translation: **p ∧ q**.
(b) 'but not' → ∧ with ¬ on q. Translation: **p ∧ ¬q**.
(c) 'not … and not …' → both ¬. Translation: **¬p ∧ ¬q**.
(d) inclusive 'or … or both' → ∨. Translation: **p ∨ q**.
flow.why_it_works: Each English connective maps cleanly; negation modifies only the piece being negated.
flow.common_mistake: Negating BOTH p and q in (b) instead of only q.

flow.title: Computing a compound truth value
flow.source_pattern: Inspired by Lab 02 Q5–Q7 — truth-value verification.
flow.problem: Build the truth table for `(p ∨ q) ∧ ¬(p ∧ q)`.
flow.approach: Add a column for each subexpression as it grows in complexity.

reveal_steps.explanation: True if at least one of p, q is true.
True only when both p and q are true.
Combine the two columns with ∧: true only when both are true.

flow.thinking_process: Build each intermediate column from the columns to its left, then combine with ∧.
step_by_step_solution: Row 1 (T, T): p ∨ q = T, p ∧ q = T, ¬(p ∧ q) = F, final = T ∧ F = **F**.
Row 2 (T, F): p ∨ q = T, p ∧ q = F, ¬(p ∧ q) = T, final = T ∧ T = **T**.
Row 3 (F, T): p ∨ q = T, p ∧ q = F, ¬(p ∧ q) = T, final = T ∧ T = **T**.
Row 4 (F, F): p ∨ q = F, p ∧ q = F, ¬(p ∧ q) = T, final = F ∧ T = **F**.
flow.final_answer: Final column read top-to-bottom: F, T, T, F. (This is exactly the truth table of p ⊕ q.)
flow.why_it_works: (p ∨ q) ∧ ¬(p ∧ q) is the textbook expansion of exclusive or — true on rows where exactly one of p, q is true.
flow.common_mistake: Computing the outer ∧ before the inner pieces, or skipping the ¬(p ∧ q) intermediate column.

flow.title: Symbolic to English
flow.source_pattern: Inspired by Lab 01 Q4 — symbolic-to-English translation.
flow.problem: Let `p` = 'Sharks have been spotted near the shore' and `q` = 'Swimming at the shore is allowed'. Translate **¬p ∨ q** to English.
flow.approach: Translate the negation first, then the disjunction, treating ∨ as inclusive.
flow.thinking_process: Build the English from the inside out.
step_by_step_solution: ¬p = 'Sharks have not been spotted near the shore.'
¬p ∨ q = 'Either no sharks have been spotted near the shore, OR swimming is allowed (or both).'
flow.final_answer: 'Either no sharks have been spotted near the shore, or swimming is allowed (or both).'
flow.why_it_works: Direct application of negation and inclusive-or definitions.
flow.common_mistake: Translating ∨ as exclusive when back-translating to English.

flow.title: Common student mistakes
items: Translating 'but' as anything other than ∧.
Reading every English 'or' as exclusive — the default in logic is inclusive (∨).
Forgetting that ¬ binds tighter than ∧ and ∨ — `¬p ∨ q` is `(¬p) ∨ q`, not `¬(p ∨ q)`.

flow.title: Four connectives, four behaviours
items: **¬** flips the bit.
**∧** is true only when **both** are true.
**∨** is true when **at least one** is true (inclusive).
**⊕** is true when **exactly one** is true (exclusive).

sections.heading: The four connectives
sections.explanation: ¬, ∧, ∨, ⊕ each have a fixed unambiguous truth table.

sections.heading: Inclusive vs exclusive 'or'
sections.explanation: Default is ∨ unless context forbids both being true.

worked_examples.problem: Let p = 'below freezing', q = 'snowing'. Translate (a) p AND q, (b) p but not q, (c) neither.
step_by_step_solution: (a) p ∧ q.
worked_examples.why_it_works: Each English connector maps cleanly to one symbol.

quick_checks.question: If p is false and q is true, what is p ∧ q?
quick_checks.explanation: Conjunction is true only when both operands are true.

quick_checks.question: Which connective best matches 'either left or right (but not both)'?
p ∨ q is true when both p and q are true.
quick_checks.explanation: Inclusive ∨ is true when at least one operand is true, including both.

key_takeaways: Conjunction (∧) is true only when both are true.
Disjunction (∨) is **inclusive** — true when at least one is true.
Exclusive or (⊕) is true when **exactly one** is true.
summary.next: Next: full **truth tables** and the trickiest connective — the conditional (→) and the biconditional (↔).

lessons.title: Truth Tables and Conditional Statements
lessons.welcome: This lesson combines two skills: building a complete **truth table** for any compound proposition, and reading the most important connective of all — the **conditional** (p → q).
objectives: Construct a complete truth table for a compound proposition with up to three atoms.
Define the implication p → q and explain why it is true when the hypothesis is false.
Translate the many English phrasings of 'if p then q' into → form.
Form the converse, contrapositive, and inverse and know which is equivalent to the original.
Define the biconditional p ↔ q and apply the standard precedence rules.
Prove a tautology using named logical equivalence laws.

storytelling.speaker: Student
storytelling.text: Why is `F → T` considered true? It feels arbitrary.

storytelling.speaker: Professor
storytelling.text: Think of p → q as a promise. The promise can only be broken on the row where p is true (the trigger fired) and q is false (the obligation failed). On any row where p is false, the promise is never tested, so we cannot say it was broken — by convention, true.

flow.title: Building a truth table — the procedure
items: 1. Count atoms n; you will need 2ⁿ rows.
2. Write a column per atom; fill all 2ⁿ truth-value combinations.
3. Add a column for each subexpression as it grows in complexity.
4. Compute each new column from the columns to its left.
5. Verify the final column row by row.

flow.title: Row counts you'll meet most often
items: 1 atom → **2** rows
2 atoms → **4** rows
3 atoms → **8** rows
4 atoms → **16** rows
5 atoms → **32** rows

flow.title: Implication (p → q)
flow.content: **p → q** is **FALSE only when p is T and q is F**. In every other row it is T.

flow.title: Implication (p → q)
flow.notes: False only when the hypothesis is true and the conclusion is false.

flow.trigger: Immediately after the implication truth table — the F→T row is the standard sticking point.

exchange.speaker: Student
exchange.text: Professor, why is `F → T` considered true?

exchange.speaker: Professor
exchange.text: Promise framing. The contract is 'if p, then q'. If p never triggers, the contract is never tested, so we say it is kept — i.e., true. The only way to break the contract is for p to trigger and q to fail.

flow.title: Implications around campus and Absher
items: _'If you submit your CPCS 222 assignment, then you receive a grade.'_ — broken only by submission + no grade.
_'If you have a valid Iqama, then you can renew your driver's license on Absher.'_ — broken only by valid Iqama + cannot renew.
_'If you scored 100 % on the final, then you get an A.'_ — broken only by 100 % + not-A.

flow.title: Many English phrases — same →
items: _'if p, then q'_
_'p implies q'_
_'p **only if** q'_
_'q if p'_
_'q whenever p'_
_'q follows from p'_
_'p is **sufficient** for q'_
_'q is **necessary** for p'_

flow.title: 'Only if' is one of the most-flipped phrases on exams
flow.content: **'p only if q'** translates to **p → q** (q is necessary for p), NOT q → p.

flow.trigger: Right after the 'only if' warning — students reliably ask this.

exchange.speaker: Student
exchange.text: Why does 'only if' reverse the direction I expect?

exchange.speaker: Professor
exchange.text: Because 'only if' marks the necessary side. 'You can enter the exam **only if** you have your student ID' means having the ID is required, so entering implies you brought the ID: `enter → have_ID`. Read 'only if' as 'requires'.

flow.title: Converse, contrapositive, inverse
items: **Converse:** q → p
**Contrapositive:** ¬q → ¬p — **logically equivalent** to p → q
**Inverse:** ¬p → ¬q — equivalent to the converse, NOT to the original

flow.title: How the four forms relate
flow.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  O["p → q (original)"] -- equivalent --> CP["¬q → ¬p (contrapositive)"]
  CV["q → p (converse)"] -- equivalent --> IN["¬p → ¬q (inverse)"]
  O -. NOT equivalent .- CV
  O -. NOT equivalent .- IN

flow.title: Biconditional (p ↔ q)
flow.content: **p ↔ q** ('p if and only if q', shortened to **iff**) is true exactly when p and q have the same truth value. Equivalently, `(p → q) ∧ (q → p)`.

flow.title: Biconditional (p ↔ q)
flow.notes: True exactly when p and q have the same truth value.

flow.title: Operator precedence (high → low)
items: 1. **¬** (tightest)
5. **↔** (loosest)

flow.title: Useful equivalences (named laws)
items: **Implication Law:** p → q ≡ ¬p ∨ q
**Biconditional Law:** p ↔ q ≡ (p → q) ∧ (q → p) ≡ (p ∧ q) ∨ (¬p ∧ ¬q)
**Negation of implication:** ¬(p → q) ≡ p ∧ ¬q

flow.title: Truth table for (p ∨ ¬q) → q
flow.source_pattern: Inspired by Lab 01 Q6 — truth-table construction.
flow.problem: Construct a complete truth table for **(p ∨ ¬q) → q** with intermediate columns.
flow.approach: Two atoms ⇒ 4 rows. Add columns for `¬q`, `p ∨ ¬q`, and finally the implication.

reveal_steps.explanation: Flip the q column row by row.
True if at least one of p, ¬q is true.
Implication is false only when p ∨ ¬q is T and q is F.

step_by_step_solution: Row 1 (T, T): ¬q = F, p ∨ ¬q = T, T → T = **T**.
Row 2 (T, F): ¬q = T, p ∨ ¬q = T, T → F = **F**.
Row 3 (F, T): ¬q = F, p ∨ ¬q = F, F → T = **T**.
Row 4 (F, F): ¬q = T, p ∨ ¬q = T, T → F = **F**.
flow.final_answer: Final column: T, F, T, F.
flow.why_it_works: Implication is false only on rows where p ∨ ¬q is T but q is F. Intermediate columns make these rows easy to spot.
flow.common_mistake: Skipping the ¬q column. With two atoms it's easy to flip a sign by accident.

flow.title: Tautology by rules — [p ∧ (p → q)] → q
flow.source_pattern: Inspired by Assignment 1 Q4 — 'Show that [p ∧ (p → q)] → q is a tautology'.
flow.problem: Show that **`[p ∧ (p → q)] → q`** is a tautology using named logical equivalence laws.
flow.approach: Eliminate the implications using the Implication Law, distribute, then simplify with the Negation, Identity, De Morgan's, Associative, and Domination Laws.

steps.explanation: Rewrite the inner implication p → q as ¬p ∨ q.
Rewrite the outer implication A → q as ¬A ∨ q.
Distribute ∧ over ∨ inside the brackets: p ∧ (¬p ∨ q) ≡ (p ∧ ¬p) ∨ (p ∧ q).
p ∧ ¬p is always false (F), by the Negation Law.
F ∨ X ≡ X, by the Identity Law (with F as the identity element of ∨).
Regroup the disjunction so ¬q and q sit together.
¬q ∨ q ≡ T (excluded middle), by the Negation Law.
X ∨ T ≡ T, by the Domination Law.

flow.conclusion: The expression simplifies to T regardless of p and q, so [p ∧ (p → q)] → q is a tautology. ∎
flow.thinking_process: Strip the implications, push negations through with De Morgan, use Negation + Identity to collapse the bracketed piece, then finish with Domination.
step_by_step_solution: Step 1: Rewrite inner → using Implication Law → [p ∧ (¬p ∨ q)] → q.
Step 2: Rewrite outer → using Implication Law → ¬[p ∧ (¬p ∨ q)] ∨ q.
Step 3: Distributive Law inside brackets → ¬[(p ∧ ¬p) ∨ (p ∧ q)] ∨ q.
Step 4: Negation Law (p ∧ ¬p ≡ F) → ¬[F ∨ (p ∧ q)] ∨ q.
Step 5: Identity Law (F ∨ X ≡ X) → ¬(p ∧ q) ∨ q.
Step 6: De Morgan's Law → (¬p ∨ ¬q) ∨ q.
Step 7: Associative Law → ¬p ∨ (¬q ∨ q).
Step 8: Negation Law (¬q ∨ q ≡ T) → ¬p ∨ T.
Step 9: Domination Law (X ∨ T ≡ T) → T.
flow.final_answer: The proposition simplifies to T. Therefore [p ∧ (p → q)] → q is a tautology. ∎
flow.why_it_works: Each step is a named logical equivalence; the chain converts the original expression into the constant T while preserving truth value at every step.
flow.common_mistake: Skipping the Associative Law in Step 7 and trying to apply Negation Law to (¬p ∨ ¬q ∨ q) without regrouping. The Negation Law requires the two literals to be next to each other inside a disjunction.

flow.title: Translating 'only if'
flow.source_pattern: Inspired by Spring 2026 midterm Q4 — translate 'access only if user is authenticated and data is encrypted'.
flow.problem: Translate: 'You can access the system **only if** you are an administrator OR you are not a freshman.' Use `a` = access, `d` = administrator, `f` = freshman.
flow.approach: Apply 'p only if q' → p → q. Identify hypothesis (a) and conclusion (d ∨ ¬f).
step_by_step_solution: Hypothesis: `a` (you can access).
Conclusion: `d ∨ ¬f` (admin OR not-a-freshman).
Combine: **a → (d ∨ ¬f)**.
flow.why_it_works: Whenever access is granted, at least one of admin / not-freshman must hold.
flow.common_mistake: Reversing into (d ∨ ¬f) → a. Read 'only if' as 'requires'.

flow.title: CCI in English (Saudi/KAU scenario)
flow.source_pattern: Inspired by Spring 2026 midterm Q3 / Assignment 1 Q3 — converse, inverse, contrapositive.
flow.problem: State the **converse, contrapositive, and inverse** of: 'If you submit the CPCS 222 assignment, then you receive a grade.'
flow.approach: Let p = submit, q = receive grade. Apply the three transformations.
flow.thinking_process: Converse swaps. Contrapositive swaps AND negates both. Inverse negates both without swapping.
step_by_step_solution: **Converse (q → p):** 'If you receive a grade, then you submitted the assignment.'
**Contrapositive (¬q → ¬p):** 'If you do not receive a grade, then you did not submit the assignment.'
**Inverse (¬p → ¬q):** 'If you do not submit the assignment, then you do not receive a grade.'
flow.final_answer:
Converse: q → p.
Contrapositive: ¬q → ¬p (logically equivalent to the original).
Inverse: ¬p → ¬q (NOT equivalent to the original).
flow.why_it_works: Mechanical application of the three definitions.
flow.common_mistake: Believing the converse follows from the original — a grade might be received another way (e.g., late credit).

flow.title: Top mistakes on exams
items: Reversing 'only if' into the wrong direction.
Treating the converse as equivalent to the original (only the contrapositive is).
Forgetting that F → anything = T (both rows with hypothesis F are true).
Writing ¬(p → q) ≡ p → ¬q. The correct form is `p ∧ ¬q`.
Skipping intermediate laws (Identity, Associative) in rule-based proofs.

flow.title: Three rules to memorize
items: **Promise rule:** an implication is broken only on T → F.
**CCI map:** **C**ontrapositive is **C**ompletely equivalent. Converse and Inverse are not.
**Iff = both arrows:** p ↔ q ≡ (p → q) ∧ (q → p).

sections.heading: Building a truth table
sections.explanation: n atoms → 2ⁿ rows; add intermediate columns; compute left-to-right.

sections.heading: The implication (→)
sections.explanation: False only on (T, F). Frame as a promise.

sections.heading: Converse, contrapositive, inverse
sections.explanation: Only the contrapositive is equivalent to the original.

sections.heading: Biconditional, precedence, named laws
sections.explanation: p ↔ q matches; precedence: ¬ > ∧ > ∨ > → > ↔; named equivalences for proofs.

worked_examples.problem: Construct a truth table for (p ∨ ¬q) → q.
step_by_step_solution: Row (T, T): ¬q = F, p ∨ ¬q = T, T → T = T.
Row (T, F): ¬q = T, p ∨ ¬q = T, T → F = F.
Row (F, T): ¬q = F, p ∨ ¬q = F, F → T = T.
Row (F, F): ¬q = T, p ∨ ¬q = T, T → F = F.
Final column: T, F, T, F.
worked_examples.why_it_works: Implication is false only when p ∨ ¬q is T but q is F.

quick_checks.question: How many rows in a truth table with 4 atoms?
Which is FALSE?
quick_checks.explanation: Implication is false only when hypothesis is T and conclusion is F.

quick_checks.question: The contrapositive of p → q is:
quick_checks.explanation: Flip and negate both parts; the contrapositive is logically equivalent to the original.

key_takeaways: A truth table with n atoms has 2ⁿ rows; build column by column.
p → q is false ONLY when p is T and q is F.
Many English phrases ('only if', 'whenever', 'sufficient', 'necessary') all translate to →.
p → q ≡ ¬q → ¬p (contrapositive); but p → q ≢ q → p (converse).
p ↔ q is true exactly when p and q have the same truth value.
Tautologies can be proven by chaining named logical equivalences (Implication, De Morgan, Distributive, Identity, Negation, Domination, etc.).

exercises.title: Module 1 Exercises — Propositional Logic
exercises.description: Practice problems modeled on CPCS 222 Labs 01–03, Assignment 1, and the Spring 2026 midterm. Includes proposition classification, truth-table construction (with structured table data), English-to-logic translation, converse/inverse/contrapositive transformations, tautology proofs using named logical equivalence laws, exam-style passages, and randomized drills.

questions.explanation: The converse is NOT equivalent.

questions.explanation: Stylistic difference only.

questions.question: Why is 'x > 5' not a proposition?
questions.answer: Because x is a free variable; without a specific value the sentence has no definite truth value.
questions.explanation: Open sentences become propositions only after their variables are bound or assigned.

questions.question: Translate to logic: 'You can enter the exam only if you have your student ID.' (e = enter, s = have ID.)
questions.explanation: 'p only if q' means p → q; the ID is necessary for entry.

questions.question: State the converse, contrapositive, and inverse of 'If it is sunny, then we go to the park.'
questions.answer:
Let p = 'it is sunny', q = 'we go to the park'. Original: p → q.
Converse (q → p): 'If we go to the park, then it is sunny.'
Contrapositive (¬q → ¬p): 'If we do not go to the park, then it is not sunny.'
Inverse (¬p → ¬q): 'If it is not sunny, then we do not go to the park.'
questions.explanation: Original p → q. Apply the three transformations. Only the contrapositive is logically equivalent to the original.
questions.source_pattern: Inspired by Spring 2026 midterm Q3 / Assignment 1 Q3.

questions.question: Use De Morgan to negate: 'It is below freezing AND it is snowing.'
questions.answer: 'It is not below freezing OR it is not snowing.'
questions.explanation: ¬(p ∧ q) ≡ ¬p ∨ ¬q by De Morgan's Law.
questions.source_pattern: Inspired by Lab 02 Q8.

questions.question: Why do we have separate symbols ∨ and ⊕ when English uses just one word, 'or'?
questions.answer: English 'or' is ambiguous between inclusive ('or both') and exclusive ('but not both'). Logic uses ∨ for inclusive and ⊕ for exclusive so every formula has exactly one meaning.
questions.explanation: Ambiguity in natural language is resolved by using two distinct symbols.

questions.question: Translate: 'If the bus AND Uber are parked at the bus station, then passengers can travel to Riyadh.' (b, u, t.)
questions.explanation: Conjunction inside the hypothesis; implication to the conclusion.
questions.source_pattern: Inspired by Assignment 1 Q2.

questions.question: p ∨ ¬p ≡ ___.

questions.question: p ∨ T ≡ ___.
questions.explanation: Domination Law.

questions.question: p ∧ T ≡ ___.
questions.explanation: Identity Law.

questions.question: Construct a complete truth table for (p ∨ q) ∧ ¬p, with one column per subexpression.

reveal_steps.explanation: Disjunction: true when at least one of p, q is true.
Conjunction of the two columns above.

questions.answer:
p | q | p∨q | ¬p | (p∨q)∧¬p
T | T |  T  | F  |    F
T | F |  T  | F  |    F
F | T |  T  | T  |    T
F | F |  F  | T  |    F
The compound is true only on (F, T).
questions.explanation: Build column by column.

questions.question: Construct a truth table for (a ⊕ ¬b) ↔ (¬a → c) with three variables.

reveal_steps.explanation: Exclusive or: true when exactly one of a, ¬b is true.
Implication: false only when ¬a is T and c is F.
Biconditional: true when the two columns match.

questions.answer: Final column read top-to-bottom: T, T, F, F, F, T, T, F.
questions.explanation: Eight rows for three variables; build intermediate columns first.
questions.source_pattern: Inspired by Assignment 1 Q1.

questions.question: Show that (p → q) ∨ (p → ¬q) is a tautology using a truth table.

reveal_steps.explanation: Implication: false only when p is T and q is F.
Implication: false only when p is T and ¬q is F.
Disjunction of the two implication columns.

questions.answer: Every row of the final column is T → tautology.
questions.explanation: When p is F both implications are vacuously T; when p is T exactly one of q, ¬q is T.

questions.question: Use logical-equivalence laws to show that ¬p → (q → r) ≡ q → (p ∨ r).

steps.explanation: Rewrite the inner implication q → r as ¬q ∨ r.
Rewrite the outer implication ¬p → A as ¬(¬p) ∨ A.
Reorder the disjunction so ¬q is on the left.

questions.answer: Equivalent. The chain of named laws transforms the left-hand side into the right.
questions.explanation: Implication Law twice + Double Negation + Associative/Commutative reordering + final Implication Law backwards.
questions.source_pattern: Inspired by Lab 03 Q5.

questions.question: Determine whether ¬(p ∨ (¬p ∧ q)) and (¬p ∧ ¬q) are equivalent using rules.
questions.conclusion: The two expressions are logically equivalent. ∎
questions.answer: Equivalent. The rule chain reduces ¬(p ∨ (¬p ∧ q)) to ¬p ∧ ¬q.
questions.explanation: De Morgan (twice), Double Negation, Distributive, Negation, Identity.
questions.source_pattern: Inspired by Lab 03 Q7.

questions.question: Are these specifications consistent? S1: 'The diagnostic message is stored OR retransmitted.' S2: 'The message is NOT stored.' S3: 'If stored, then retransmitted.'
questions.answer:
**Let:**
p = the message is stored
q = the message is retransmitted

**Specifications:**
S1: p ∨ q
S2: ¬p
S3: p → q

**Try:**
p = F, q = T

**Check:**
S1 = F ∨ T = T ✓
S2 = ¬F = T ✓
S3 = F → T = T (vacuous) ✓

**Conclusion:**
All three specifications are true under this assignment, so the specifications are CONSISTENT.
questions.explanation: Find one assignment that makes every spec true. If none exists, the spec list is inconsistent.
questions.source_pattern: Inspired by Lab 02 Q9 — consistency check.

questions.question: Read the passage and identify the non-propositions.
questions.passage: Sara arrived at KAU before her CPCS 222 lecture. The library opens at 7:30 AM. Please silence your phone. 12 is divisible by 4. She wrote x + 5 = 11 in her notebook. Wow, the lecture hall is full today!

sentences.sentence: Sara arrived at KAU before her CPCS 222 lecture.

sentences.explanation: Free variable x — truth depends on x.

sentences.sentence: Wow, the lecture hall is full today!

questions.answer: Non-propositions: 'Please silence your phone' (command), 'x + 5 = 11' (open sentence), 'Wow, the lecture hall is full today!' (exclamation).
questions.explanation: Each fails one of the two property checks.

questions.question: For the sentence 'Having a valid student ID is necessary for entering the exam', state inverse, converse, contrapositive in English. (s = valid ID, e = enter the exam.)
questions.answer:
**Translation:** 'necessary' marks the conclusion, so e → s (entering implies having the ID).

**Converse (s → e):** 'If you have a valid student ID, then you can enter the exam.'

**Contrapositive (¬s → ¬e):** 'If you do not have a valid student ID, then you cannot enter the exam.' (equivalent to the original)

**Inverse (¬e → ¬s):** 'If you cannot enter the exam, then you do not have a valid student ID.' (equivalent to the converse, not the original)
questions.explanation: 'Necessary' marks the conclusion of an implication.
questions.source_pattern: Inspired by Spring 2026 midterm Q3 — CCI in English.

questions.question: Translate: 'Access is granted only if the user is authenticated AND the data is encrypted.' (s = access granted, q = authenticated, r = encrypted.)
questions.answer:
**'p only if q'** ⇒ p → q. Here p = s (access granted), q = (q ∧ r).

**Translation:** s → (q ∧ r).
questions.explanation: 'Only if' marks the right-hand side as the necessary condition.
questions.source_pattern: Inspired by Spring 2026 midterm Q4.

questions.question: Translate: 'The system is secure if and only if either the data is encrypted or the user is authenticated, but not both.' (p, q, r as above.)
questions.answer:
**Translation:** p ↔ (q ⊕ r).

**Why:** 'if and only if' is ↔; 'either … or … but not both' is exclusive or ⊕.
questions.explanation: Two connectives — ↔ and ⊕.
questions.source_pattern: Inspired by Spring 2026 midterm Q4 second sub-question.

questions.question: Show that [p ∧ (p → q)] → q is a tautology using rules of equivalence (not a truth table).

steps.explanation: Rewrite inner p → q as ¬p ∨ q.
Rewrite outer A → q as ¬A ∨ q.
Regroup so ¬q and q sit together.

questions.conclusion: The proposition simplifies to T regardless of p and q; therefore it is a tautology. ∎
questions.explanation: Each step cites the exact CPCS222 law name.
questions.source_pattern: Inspired by Assignment 1 Q4.
